content: Ragwort, scientifically known as Senecio jacobaea, is a prevalent wildflower belonging to the Asteraceae family. It is native to Europe, where it thrives in dry, open areas, and has also spread as a weed to other regions. In North America, a related species is Packera obovata. Ragwort is known by various names, including Cushag (Isle of Man), Buachalán Buí (Ireland), Tansy Ragwort, St. James-wort, Ragweed, Stinking Nanny/Ninny/Willy, Staggerwort, Dog Standard, Cankerwort, Stammerwort, and Mare's Fart. In the western United States, it is often referred to as Tansy Ragwort or simply Tansy, though this is misleading as its resemblance to true tansy is superficial. This misnaming is potentially hazardous, as true tansy has culinary uses. Botanical Description Ragwort is a biennial or perennial plant. Its leaves are pinnately lobed, with the terminal lobe being blunt. The plant emits an unpleasant odor, which is the origin of some of its more colorful names, such as Stinking Nanny and Mare's Fart. Its flowers are bright yellow, approximately 1.5 cm in diameter, and grow in dense, flat-topped clusters. Ragwort has an extended flowering period from June to November and is pollinated by a variety of bees, flies, moths, and butterflies. A single plant can produce between 2,000 and 2,500 flowers in 20to 60-headed corymbs, yielding between 75,000 and 200,000 seeds. However, in its native Eurasian range, most seeds do not travel far from the parent plant, and only a small fraction germinate into new plants. Taxonomy Two subspecies of Senecio jacobaea are recognized: Senecio jacobaea ssp. jacobaea: The typical form with ray florets. Senecio jacobaea ssp. dunensis: A form lacking ray florets. Distribution Ragwort is commonly found along roadsides, waste grounds, and in areas with cool climates and high rainfall. It is native to Eurasia, where it is widespread from Scandinavia to the Mediterranean. In Britain and Ireland, it is classified as a weed. In the United States, it has been introduced and is primarily found in the Northwest and Northeast, including states such as California, Oregon, Washington, and New York. It also grows in Argentina, northern Africa, India, Siberia, New Zealand, and Australia. In New Zealand and many Australian states, ragwort is considered a noxious weed, requiring landowners to remove it by law. In New Zealand, farmers sometimes use helicopters to spray large infestations. Biological Control Ragwort serves as a food source for the larvae of several insects, including Cochylis atricapitana, Phycitodes maritima, and Phycitodes saxicolais. It is most notably associated with the cinnabar moth (Tyria jacobaeae), whose caterpillars absorb alkaloids from the plant, making them unpalatable to predators. The moth's black and yellow warning colors, as well as the red and black coloration of the adult moth, signal their toxicity. The cinnabar moth has been introduced as a biological control agent in countries like New Zealand and the western United States, where ragwort has become problematic. In New Zealand, the ragwort flea beetle (Longitarsus jacobaeae) has also been introduced to combat the plant. Additionally, ragwort is a host plant for Longitarsus ganglbauri. Toxicity and Poisonous Effects Ragwort contains numerous alkaloids, including pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs), which are toxic to animals and humans. The World Health Organization (WHO) has reported that these alkaloids can cause liver damage and are potentially fatal. Alkaloids confirmed in the plant include jacobine, jaconine, jacozine, otosenine, retrorsine, seneciphylline, senecionine, and senkirkinine. Other alkaloids, such as acetyl erucifoline and riddelline, have also been reported. Ragwort poses a significant risk to livestock, particularly horses and cattle. In regions where ragwort is native, such as Britain and continental Europe, documented cases of poisoning are rare, as symptoms may only appear months after ingestion. Horses typically avoid ragwort due to its bitter taste, but if consumed in sufficient quantities, it can cause irreversible liver cirrhosis. Symptoms of poisoning in horses include yellow mucus membranes, depression, and lack of coordination. Animals may resort to eating ragwort during food shortages, and in rare cases, they can develop a preference for it. Sheep, in contrast, consume small amounts of ragwort with apparent relish, and some reports suggest that the alkaloids may help kill stomach worms. However, the WHO warns that sheep and goats also suffer liver damage, albeit at a slower rate than horses and pigs. The danger of ragwort lies in the cumulative effect of its toxins. While the alkaloids themselves do not accumulate in the liver, their breakdown products can damage DNA and progressively kill liver cells. A lethal dose for horses is sometimes cited as 3-7% of their body weight, though there are documented cases of horses surviving after consuming over 20% of their body weight. The WHO emphasizes that frequent ingestion of small doses is as harmful as consuming a single lethal dose. Humans using herbal remedies containing PAs are at high risk of death within 18-24 months due to liver damage. The effects of low doses may be mitigated by bacterial action in the digestive tract, which destroys the original alkaloids before they enter the bloodstream. There is no known antidote or cure for ragwort poisoning, though cessation of consumption has led to recovery in some cases. Honey collected from ragwort flowers has been found to contain small amounts of alkaloids such as jacoline, jacobine, and senecionine. Control Legislation In the Republic of Ireland, ragwort is classified as a noxious weed under the Noxious Weeds Act of 1936, requiring landowners to control its growth. In the United Kingdom, common ragwort is listed as an injurious weed under the Weeds Act of 1959. This designation indicates its potential harm to agriculture rather than its toxicity to animals. Land occupiers can be required to prevent its spread, but there is no general legal obligation for landowners to control it. The Ragwort Control Act of 2003 introduced a code of practice for managing ragwort but did not impose additional legal responsibilities on landowners. Historical and Medicinal Uses Historically, ragwort was used externally to treat eye inflammations, ulcers, rheumatism, sciatica, gout, and joint pain. It was also believed to relieve bee stings. All applications were external and required professional supervision. Due to its pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which inhibit cell division, some researchers hope to explore its potential in slowing or arresting cancer cell growth. Other Uses In ancient Greece and Rome, ragwort was used to create a supposed aphrodisiac called satyrion. Its leaves can produce a green dye, while its flowers yield yellow, brown, or orange dyes. Prominent herbalists like Gerard and Culpeper recommended the plant, and it has been celebrated in poetry, such as John Clare's 1831 poem and Josephine Kermode's poem about the Cushag. Cultivation Ragwort is not cultivated, and no known varieties exist. Trivia Ragwort is sometimes mistakenly referred to as the national flower of the Isle of Man, where it is known as Cushag.
